name: Fatima Kowalski

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Good evening, Fatima, and thank you for seeing me before your shift. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government, and what you say is confidential. Could you describe a normal working night?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run the oven line at Golden Crust, the big bakery on the ring road. We do sliced bread and rolls for the supermarkets, about forty thousand loaves a night. I start at ten, check the proofer, that's the warm room where the dough rises, then I set the oven zones and watch the colour of the crust all night. If the bake's wrong, two hours of bread goes in the skip, so I don't take my eyes off it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about the work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it matters. Families eat what I bake at breakfast. My grandmother baked bread by hand in her village, and I tell her I bake forty thousand a night and she laughs. What's hard is the nights, and the pay. I'm the senior on the line and I'm still on less than the day supervisors, and there's no other bakery like this for fifty kilometres.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. I never trusted all that talk anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what my father says: hard work doesn't go out of fashion. At work I'd tell the young ones to stop worrying about computers and learn the ovens properly. I don't post things online. I'd say it after church, maybe, if anyone asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means things stay hard but honest. I have less than a month of money saved, and Piotr (my fiancé), who's an electrician's apprentice, and I are saving for the wedding in June. The night premium is what makes the money work, and Golden Crust keeps talking about cutting it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working nights and do every extra shift I'm offered. I'd ask my uncle if Piotr and I could rent his upstairs flat cheaper after the wedding. And I'd keep the wedding small, sixty people at the parish hall, not a hotel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady. Tired, but steady. I trust God and my own hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said they talk about cutting the night premium. What happens if they do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I lose about a hundred and fifty a month. We'd still marry in June, I'm not moving that. But we'd live at my uncle's and the honeymoon would be a weekend at the lake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you look at AI tools for anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I've never used them and I don't need to. My mother runs the house on a notebook and it works fine.

say: She'd say **hard work** doesn't go out of fashion.
Young bakers should **learn the ovens** properly instead of worrying about computers.
think: Things stay **hard but honest**, with under a month saved.
Golden Crust keeps talking about cutting the **night premium**.
do: Ask her uncle about renting his **upstairs flat** cheaply.
Keep the wedding to **sixty guests** at the parish hall.
feel: **Tired but steady**, trusting her faith and her own hands.
S0.quote: Hard work doesn't go out of fashion.
fieldNote: Her worry is the **night premium**, worth about a hundred and fifty a month.
She leans on **family and church**, not on government or tools.
The **June wedding** is fixed; everything else bends around it.

steps.text: Take every extra night shift at Golden Crust
Ask her uncle to rent them his upstairs flat cheaply
Hold a sixty-guest wedding at the parish hall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So the office people change first. Fine by me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the bakery will always need bakers, and the offices were too big anyway. That's what I'd say at the canteen. I'd tell my brother, who works in an insurance office, to start looking around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I'm not sure the ovens are safe forever. They already have a robot arm stacking trays in the dispatch area. If the planning goes to a computer, it'll push the line faster, and the people upstairs who know us will be gone. That worries me more than I'd say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my job better than anyone, so they keep me. I'd cut our wedding budget again and put the difference in savings, maybe five hundred. I wouldn't learn the AI things. If they make me use a new screen, I'll learn that screen and nothing more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like the oven's running a degree hot and nobody else has noticed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You told your brother to look around. What would you tell yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: To be the best on the line. The bakery won't let go of the person who stops the bread burning. At least not soon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone at the bakery you'd worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mr Novak, the shift planner. He's sixty-one and he does it all from memory and paper. A computer would replace him in a week, and he's been there thirty years.

say: The bakery will always need **bakers**, and offices were **too big** anyway.
She'd tell her brother in insurance to **start looking**.
think: A **robot arm** already stacks trays in dispatch.
Planning software would **push the line** faster and remove managers who know them.
do: Do her job **better than anyone** so they keep her.
Cut the **wedding budget** and save about five hundred.
Learn **only the screens** she's required to use.
feel: **Uneasy**, like an oven running a degree hot unnoticed.
S1.quote: The bakery won't let go of the person who stops the bread burning.
fieldNote: Public **confidence** hides private doubt about the robot arm in dispatch.
She **resists AI** firmly but would learn a required screen.
She worries for **Mr Novak**, an older planner done on paper.

steps.text: Keep the oven line's waste the lowest in the bakery
Cut five hundred from the wedding budget into savings
Wait to learn new screens until Golden Crust requires it

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In two years? God help us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is men in big companies chasing money without thinking of families. I wouldn't ask for handouts, I'd say the companies should keep people working. I'd say that to anyone who'd listen, even online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the bakery gets the robots by 2031, because bread is the same thing every night and machines like that. I'd be thirty-one, married, maybe with a baby, and no job. That's the part that frightens me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk with Piotr about waiting for children until we know what's happening, which breaks my heart. I'd ask my parents if we could live with them for a while to save. And I'd ask my uncle about working in his butcher's shop, because people still want a person behind the counter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. I'd pray more, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Piotr is an electrician's apprentice. How does his work look?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Better than mine, I think. Robots need wiring, and old houses need fixing. If anyone in our house has work in 2031, it's him. That's not how I pictured it, but I'd be grateful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said no handouts. If things got very bad, would you take government help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For a little while, if I had to. But I'd rather it came from my family and my parish first. That's how my parents got through bad years.

Companies should **keep people working** instead of offering handouts.
think: Bread is repetitive, so **robots come by 2031**.
She'd be thirty-one, married, maybe with **a baby**, and no job.
do: Ask her **parents** if they can live with them to save.
Ask her uncle about work in his **butcher's shop**.
S2.quote: Bread is the same thing every night and machines like that.
fieldNote: She blames **big companies**, not government, and rejects handouts in principle.
**Delaying children** is the most painful change she names.
She expects her fiancé's **electrical trade** to outlast her job.

steps.text: Talk with Piotr about delaying children
Move in with her parents to save rent
Ask her uncle for counter work at his butcher's shop

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's a little more breathing room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have time to prepare, so families should pull together. At work I'd say the young ones should learn a trade with their hands that robots won't do soon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd probably do too little, because I don't like change. I'd keep baking until 2031 and then say there are still three years. That's how I am. Piotr would push me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working nights at Golden Crust and save the night premium every month into a separate account. We'd still get married in June. And I'd help at my uncle's butcher's on Saturdays, just to learn, without giving up the bakery.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but I'd keep it to myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Piotr would push you. How?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd sit me down with a pen and paper and make a list. He likes lists. I'd complain and then I'd do what's on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about children in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd still try in a year or two. Five years is enough for a child to start school. I don't want to stop living because of machines.

say: Families should **pull together** while there's time.
Young people should learn a **hands-on trade** robots won't do soon.
think: She'd **do too little**, because she dislikes change.
Her fiancé **Piotr** would have to sit her down and push her to act.
do: Save the **night premium** monthly in a separate account.
Help at her uncle's **butcher's** on Saturdays to learn.
S3.quote: I don't want to stop living because of machines.
fieldNote: She knows her own **resistance** and relies on her fiancé to push her.
Five years lets her keep **family plans**, including children.
She tests a **new trade** quietly while keeping the bakery.

steps.text: Save the night premium in a separate account each month
Help at her uncle's butcher's shop on Saturdays
Try for a first child within two years

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's nearly forever for a bakery.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and people should stop scaring each other. I'd say the companies and the churches and families will work it out between them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd do nothing at all for most of it. That's the danger. The robots would come when I'm thirty-seven, with children in school, and I'd still be on the oven line saying there's time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my job and my routine. We'd get married, try for a baby, and maybe buy a small house near my parents if the bank allowed it. I'd ask my uncle to teach me the butcher's trade properly over a few years, so I have something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm. A small worry at the back, like a timer you can't see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said buy a house. Is that wise if the job might go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe not. But my parents bought when they had nothing and they managed. With family close, you always manage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you act sooner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A robot on the oven itself, not just in dispatch. The day I see a robot on the oven line itself, I'd go to my uncle the next morning.

say: Ten years is a **long time**, so people should stop scaring each other.
Companies, **churches and families** will work it out between them.
think: She'd likely **do nothing** for most of the decade.
Robots arrive when she's **thirty-seven** with children in school.
do: Keep her **job and routine** at Golden Crust.
Marry, try for **a baby**, and maybe buy a house near her parents.
Learn the **butcher's trade** from her uncle over a few years.
S4.quote: The day I see a robot on the oven line itself, I'd go to my uncle the next morning.
fieldNote: She names a clear **trigger**: a robot on the oven line.
Long warning brings **life plans** forward, not career change.
She trusts **family closeness** over financial caution.

steps.text: Keep running the oven line on nights
Try for a baby and look for a small house near her parents
Learn the butcher's trade from her uncle over a few years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Married with no savings, and the bakery gone by 2031. What would help is companies having to keep people on and teach them new work, and apprenticeships for adults, not just teenagers. And family, always family.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about faith. People will need it. When the work goes, people need somewhere to go on a Sunday that tells them they're still worth something.

headlineQuote: When the work goes, people need somewhere to go on a Sunday that tells them they're still worth something.
portrait: Fatima is a **27-year-old** senior oven-line operator on nights at Golden Crust, a large bakery.
She's engaged to Piotr, an **electrician's apprentice**, with a June wedding and under a month saved.
**Traditional** in outlook, she trusts work, faith and family over government help.
She **never uses AI** and admits she'd delay acting until she sees a robot on her line.
Short warnings make her consider **delaying children**; long ones bring family plans forward.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**: married, no savings, and the bakery automated by 2031.
whatWouldHelp: **Adult apprenticeships** and companies required to **retrain staff**.
